Displaying Surfaces with RGL

Bradley Buchsbaum

2026-11-12

Source: vignettes/articles/displaying-surfaces.Rmd
displaying-surfaces.Rmd

This vignette shows how to display cortical geometry, curvature, and vertex values with RGL. It uses the small std.8 surfaces bundled with neurosurf, so no downloads are needed. Every RGL scene below is an interactive WebGL widget: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom. Static figures use neurosurf’s CPU renderer, which needs no OpenGL.

The std.8 template has 642 vertices per hemisphere, about 10 mm apart. RGL colours each vertex and blends across triangles, so on a mesh this coarse a thresholded map gets jagged edges. One round of Loop subdivision (2,562 vertices) and the fade view_surface() applies at the threshold keep them smooth enough for display:

library(neurosurf)

refine <- function(geometry) {
  mesh <- Rvcg::vcgSubdivide(geometry@mesh, threshold = 0,
                             type = "Loop", iterations = 1,
                             silent = TRUE)
  SurfaceGeometry(t(mesh$vb[1:3, ]), t(mesh$it) - 1L, geometry@hemi)
}
std8 <- load_fsaverage_std8("smoothwm")
left <- refine(std8$lh)
right <- refine(std8$rh)
inflated_lh <- refine(load_fsaverage_std8("inflated")$lh)
anatomy <- curvature(left)

For values, two smooth clusters of opposite sign stand in for a statistic map. Each is placed at a surface coordinate and falls off with distance over the inflated surface, which follows the cortical sheet:

blob <- function(centre, peak, width = 15) {
  seed <- which.min(colSums((t(coords(left)) - centre)^2))
  xyz <- coords(inflated_lh)
  peak * exp(-colSums((t(xyz) - xyz[seed, ])^2) / (2 * width^2))
}
vertex_values <- blob(c(-45, -60, 20), 3) +  # parietal, positive
  blob(c(-55, -20, 0), -2.5)                 # temporal, negative

Open a scene and show it

view_surface() draws into the current RGL device when new_window = FALSE. This helper gives each example a private NULL device, returns the scene as a WebGL widget, and closes the device even if the plotting call fails. In an interactive session, use rgl::open3d() to get a desktop window instead.

with_rgl_scene <- function(code) {
  device <- rgl::open3d(useNULL = TRUE)
  on.exit(rgl::close3d(device), add = TRUE)
  force(code)
  rgl::rglwidget()
}

A SurfaceGeometry records its hemisphere, so viewpoint = "lateral" selects the appropriate left or right view. By default the surface is shaded by its curvature, sulci dark and gyri light; bgcol replaces that base colour.

with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, viewpoint = "lateral", zoom = 0.7,
               new_window = FALSE)
)

Overlay values

Pass vertex values in vals. irange sets the colour limits and thresh = c(-1, 1) leaves values inside that band uncoloured, so the curvature shows through; colour fades in just past the threshold. Signed values get neurosurf’s diverging palette, surface_palette("two_sided"): blue below zero, red above, with no white centre to fade into the grey anatomy. Pass cmap to choose another.

with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, vals = vertex_values, irange = c(-3, 3),
               thresh = c(-1, 1), viewpoint = "lateral", zoom = 0.7,
               new_window = FALSE)
)

Colour limits are ±3 and |value| < 1 is uncoloured: blue negative, red positive. On a folded surface parts of each cluster lie in sulcal banks hidden from this view, so their edges look clipped; statistical maps are usually shown on the inflated surface, as in [Publication-quality surface figures](https://bbuchsbaum.github.io/neurosurf/articles/surface-figures.html). For a static figure with a colour key, use surface_figure(). It renders the same values with the CPU renderer, which interpolates within each triangle, so its lighting and colour mapping do not depend on RGL.

figure <- surface_figure(
  lh = left, values = vertex_values, anatomy = anatomy,
  views = "lateral", threshold = 1, limits = c(-3, 3),
  alpha_ramp = 0.25, legend_title = "value",
  panel_width = 680, panel_height = 400, antialias = 2
)

Vertex colours

vert_clrs supplies one explicit colour per vertex and overrides scalar colour mapping, for example to show a parcellation. Here the anterior half of the hemisphere (positive y) is green and the posterior half purple. alpha blends these colours with the curvature shading beneath, so the folds stay visible.

y <- coords(left)[, 2]
halves <- ifelse(y > median(y), "#1b7837", "#762a83")
with_rgl_scene(
  view_surface(left, vert_clrs = halves, alpha = 0.6,
               viewpoint = "lateral", zoom = 0.7, new_window = FALSE)
)

specular sets the highlight colour (the default "black" gives a matte surface), and lit turns lighting on or off. These change the displayed scene, not the stored geometry or vertex data.

Combine hemispheres in one scene

The two lateral surfaces face opposite directions, so show them in separate panels. A dorsal view sees both hemispheres at once, so they can share one scene; offset separates them along x. Anterior is at the top.

with_rgl_scene({
  view_surface(left, viewpoint = "dorsal", offset = c(-5, 0, 0),
               new_window = FALSE)
  view_surface(right, viewpoint = "dorsal", offset = c(5, 0, 0),
               zoom = 0.75, new_window = FALSE)
})

Other views are "medial", "ventral", "anterior" and "posterior". For static multi-view output, surface_figure() combines hemispheres and labels each view; see [Publication-quality surface figures](https://bbuchsbaum.github.io/neurosurf/articles/surface-figures.html).

Mark vertices and plot a surface data object

NeuroSurface stores values with the vertex indices they belong to (it can also hold a subset of vertices). Its plot() method passes them to view_surface(), so the same threshold and fade apply. Markers refer to vertices too: these sit on the peak vertex of each cluster.

surface <- NeuroSurface(left, indices = nodes(left),
                        data = vertex_values)
peaks <- data.frame(
  vertex = c(which.max(vertex_values), which.min(vertex_values)),
  radius = 2.5, color = "#1f2933"
)
with_rgl_scene(
  plot(surface, irange = c(-3, 3), thresh = c(-1, 1),
       spheres = peaks,
       spheres_as_vertices = TRUE, viewpoint = "lateral", zoom = 0.7,
       new_window = FALSE)
)

Smooth and threshold a noisy map

Smoothing and cluster-size thresholding operate on surface data before rendering. Here noise is added to the two clusters, averaged over a 5 mm geodesic radius (sigma), and thresholded at |value| > 1. Smoothing recovers the two known clusters but leaves small specks of noise; cluster_threshold() removes every connected cluster smaller than 20 vertices.

set.seed(123)
noise <- rnorm(length(vertex_values))
noisy <- NeuroSurface(left, indices = nodes(left),
                      data = vertex_values + noise)
smoothed <- smooth(noisy, sigma = 5)
clustered <- cluster_threshold(smoothed, size = 20,
                               threshold = c(-1, 1))

Shown as small multiples with the same colour scale. surface_panels() lays out rendered panels in a row with labels and the shared key:

steps <- list(noisy = noisy, smoothed = smoothed,
              clustered = clustered)
panels <- lapply(steps, function(x) {
  render_surface_rgba(left, as.numeric(x@data),
                      anatomy_metric = anatomy,
                      camera = "lateral", threshold = 1,
                      limits = c(-3, 3), width = 420, height = 260,
                      antialias = 2)
})
surface_panels(panels, legend_title = "value")

surface_montage() lays out RGL snapshots the same way; it needs a rendering backend, so it is not run here:

surface_montage(list(noisy, smoothed, clustered), irange = c(-3, 3),
                thresh = c(-1, 1), ncol = 3)

Save an RGL snapshot

snapshot_surface() saves a PNG through the available RGL rendering backend. On a NULL device it needs webshot2 and a headless browser, and it returns an empty path when no snapshot could be made. Building this article does not launch a browser, so this recipe is not run here:

file <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
path <- snapshot_surface(left, file = file, vals = vertex_values,
                         irange = c(-3, 3), viewpoint = "lateral")

For browser-free PNG output, use surface_figure() or render_surface_rgba(). For interactive reports with several selectable maps, see [Build bilateral interactive surface reports](https://bbuchsbaum.github.io/neurosurf/articles/interactive-surfaces.html).

The bundled templates retain the FreeSurfer terms in system.file("extdata", "LICENSE-FreeSurfer.txt", package = "neurosurf").
